summary: The note examines how space agencies responded to a significant solar flare on September 23, 2023, which caused an S3 (strong) radiation storm. It describes the radiation protocols and emphases of NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, CNSA, JAXA and the CSA, comparing common elements and differences. It closes by looking at how radiation protection will evolve for future Moon and Mars missions.
one_line: Overview of how NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, CNSA, JAXA and CSA responded to the September 23, 2023 solar flare and radiation storm, and what it means for mission safety.
key_facts: On September 23, 2023, a significant solar flare produced a radiation storm classified as S3 (strong) on the NOAA Space Weather Scales.
Space weather includes solar flares, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and high-speed solar wind streams, which affect satellites, electrical grids and astronaut safety.
Dr. Jane Thompson, a space weather expert, said "The September event proves we are never completely prepared for what the Sun can unleash."
NASA's radiation protocols include real-time monitoring of radiation levels, safe havens on spacecraft, and personal dosimeters.
ISS astronauts followed standard procedure by moving to the station's more shielded modules while staying in continual communication with mission control.
NASA limits the time astronauts spend in high-risk areas during ExtraVehicular Activities (EVAs) through pre-flight planning and operational constraints.
Roscosmos shared data from its spacecraft and leveraged its ISS partnership; spokesperson Dmitri Volkov stressed working with international partners on the ISS.
ESA takes a research-centric approach, relying on advanced space weather monitoring systems; safety officer Theresa Schmitt called the data collected "invaluable."
CNSA has a rapidly developing protocol with emergency procedures similar to those of other leading agencies.
JAXA's strategy integrates continual space weather updates, deployment of shielding materials, and post-mission health monitoring.
The Canadian Space Agency has no astronaut corps in this account but supported monitoring through its RADARSAT satellites.
NASA and Roscosmos invest heavily in real-time response systems, while ESA and JAXA emphasize research and post-mission care.
Future work includes new spacecraft shielding materials, space weather forecasting models, and biological countermeasures for Moon and Mars missions.
